sections.title: What it is
sections.html:
#What it is

orbit-launcher is the full-screen terminal program that installs, updates, repairs and removes Orbit on the server that hosts it. Orbit's install line downloads it, checks it and starts it for you.

sections.title: What you need
sections.html:
#What you need

  • A Linux server. Orbit's download script stops on any other system, and on anything but 64-bit x86 or arm64. Orbit itself is built for 64-bit x86 (amd64) only for now, so use amd64. The launcher is tested by installing Orbit on Ubuntu and on Fedora.
  • Docker with Compose v2. Plus curl, openssl, tar, sha256sum, base64 and GNU timeout, which most Linux systems already have.
  • A normal user account that can use Docker. The launcher refuses to run as root, with or without sudo.
  • Memory. The launcher counts 6 GiB for Standard: Orbit's 2 GiB and the malware scanner's 4 GiB memory limits. The database and the system need memory on top of that. Documents adds a 1 GiB attachment reader, 7 GiB in all. The launcher reads the machine's total memory on Linux and will not start Documents when it is under 7 GiB. It never blocks Standard.
  • Ports. Orbit listens on port 3000 on every network interface unless you change ORBIT_PORT or ORBIT_BIND_ADDRESS in .env-orbit. Put an HTTPS reverse proxy in front of it. Never expose Orbit directly to the internet. Installing Orbit covers the proxy.
  • Disk. No minimum is documented. If Orbit fails to start, the installer reports the free space on the install folder and on Docker's data folder.
  • Internet access to GitHub (the install files and the launcher's update check), to GitHub's container registry (ghcr.io, for Orbit's image) and to Docker Hub (for the database, scanner and attachment-reader images). While Orbit runs, the scanner also downloads its signature updates. Set ORBIT_LAUNCHER_NO_UPDATE_CHECK to any non-empty value to skip the launcher's update check.

sections.title: Install, then claim
sections.html:
#Install, then claim

The short version. Installing Orbit has the full requirements and explains the sign-in questions. Its menu and profile names are those of Orbit's plain installer, not the launcher's.

  1. Set up the HTTPS reverse proxy for Orbit's public address first (Installing Orbit covers its settings). The claim link opens that address, so it must already reach Orbit on port 3000.
  2. Make an empty folder for Orbit and open a terminal in it. The launcher works on the folder it is started from.
  3. Run the install line from Installing Orbit. It checks the signed release and starts the launcher.
  4. Choose Install, then a profile: Standard or Documents. The Agent and Full rows show "not yet".
  5. Read the note about Orbit's state and risks. After a 20-second countdown, and once you have scrolled to the end, type I've read this and I understand to go on.
  6. Watch the install run in the launcher's console. Orbit then asks for its settings (its public address, how people sign in) in that console, or briefly hands you the terminal to answer.
  7. On the final screen, the address shows as alive and unclaimed. Choose Get into Orbit to open the claim link, or Copy claim link if the server has no browser (your terminal must allow clipboard writes). Whoever opens the link first creates the first administrator, so open it yourself. If no link shows, run docker compose --env-file .env-orbit logs orbit-app in the folder and open the link Orbit printed.

After that, export a recovery bundle, as Installing Orbit explains.

sections.title: Update and Repair
sections.html:
#Update and Repair

Run the install line again from the Orbit folder and choose:

  • Update pulls the latest Orbit and updates this deployment, keeping its configuration. The launcher takes no backup, and Orbit's note says an upgrade may not keep your data, so back up first (see the link at the end). One-step update with a backup, a health check and rollback is planned (issue #317 in the launcher's GitLab project, update in one step).
  • Repair runs the deployment's own scripts/repair.sh to diagnose it and shows what a fix would do. It changes nothing until you agree, and offers only the actions the plan proposes. It cannot yet start services that failed to start: issue #256 in the launcher's GitLab project.

sections.title: What Remove deletes
sections.html:
#What Remove deletes

Remove works in two steps, and the launcher runs only the first.

  1. Stand down (the launcher runs this after you confirm). It runs docker compose down: it stops Orbit and removes its containers and network. It deletes no files, no data volumes and no images.
  2. The removal command (you decide whether to run it). The launcher shows a command and offers to copy it, but never runs it. It is docker compose … down -v && sudo rm -rf <your Orbit folder>. It deletes the data volumes (the database, with its mail, and the documents and scanner volumes) and the whole folder: configuration, secrets, backups and anything else you put there. It cannot be undone. It leaves Docker images alone.

If the folder is the root folder or your home folder, the launcher offers only the data-volume half and leaves the folder for you. Removing the data volumes matters: a database volume left behind makes a later install stop.

Remove acts only on the Orbit found in the folder you start the launcher in. A change so that Remove deletes only Orbit's own files, and keeps everything else in the folder, is planned: issue #285 in the launcher's GitLab project.

sections.title: Options
sections.html:
#Options

orbit-launcher --version prints its version. orbit-launcher --licences prints the licences of what it includes. ORBIT_LAUNCHER_NO_ANIMATION, set to any non-empty value, skips the opening animation.

sections.title: For contributors
sections.html:
#For contributors

The launcher is not currently taking outside code changes: see CONTRIBUTING.md. Build it with go build ./cmd/orbit-launcher and test it with go test -race ./.... docs/releasing.md says how releases are made and docs/implementation-plan.md describes the code. Orbit builds and signs the launcher with each Orbit release; this repository holds its source, tests and version tags.

TestLive_UpdateExistingDeployment (build tag live, #331) updates a deployment somebody else installed and leaves it running, for Orbit's upgrade cell (ai/orbit#1666). It is skipped unless ORBIT_LIVE_EXISTING_DIR is set; then ORBIT_RELEASE_MANIFEST, ORBIT_LAUNCHER_LIVE_BINARY and ORBIT_LAUNCHER_INSTALL_SCRIPT_PATH (or _URL) are required, and ORBIT_LAUNCHER_LIVE_RAW_LOG is optional. See issue #331 for the interface.
